We test several state-of-the-art agricultural VLN agents on it and observe a sufficient drop with -57 on SR and -9 on NE, from which we suggest that an agricultural VLN agent tends to assume that the given instruction is correct, so does not have the awareness to doubt it when the scenes it sees do not align with the instruction it receives. To build the awareness on instruction mistake, we propose the IMAC module analyzing the instruction and the current front-facing image, to judge whether the instruction has mistakes and attempt to correct it when needed. We integrate IMAC into the baseline model, and observe a noteworthy improvement, sufficiently narrowing the gap to the performance on instructions without mistakes. Project: https://github.com/AlexTraveling/IMAC-AgriVLN . Introduction Agricultural robots are serving as powerful assistants across a wide range of tasks, such as laser weeding COMPAG:LaserWeeding , growth monitoring RAL:GrowthMonitoring and cross-pollination Cell:Pollination . However, most of them still heavily rely on manual operations or railway systems for movement, resulting in limited mobility and poor adaptability. In contrast, Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) enables agents to follow the natural language instructions to navigate to the target positions CVPR:R2R,ECCV:VLN-CE , having demonstrated strong performance across various domains TMLR , such as R2R CVPR:R2R for indoor rooms, TOUCHDOWN CVPR:TOUCHDOWN for urban streets, and AerialVLN ICCV:AerialVLN for aerial spaces. Motivated by prior Vision-Language Model-based approaches AAAI:NavGPT,ACL:MapGPT,ICRA:Discuss , Zhao et al. arXiv:AgriVLN proposed the AgriVLN method and the A2A benchmark to pioneeringly extend VLN to the agricultural domain, enabling agricultural robots to navigate to the target positions following the natural language instructions. However, almost all the prior methods ICCV:YouTube,AAAI:VELMA,CVPR:OVER-NAV,ACL:BabyWalk,ICCV:VLN-PETL,AAAI:VLN-VIDEO , including AgriVLN, adopt an ideal assumption that the given instructions themselves are correct, which does not align with the realistic scenarios, because anybody may say an instruction with mistakes, as illustrated in Figure fig:teaser . If the decision-maker was a human, which had the subconsciousness to doubt whether the instruction has mistakes when the scenes it sees does not align with the instruction it receives. This phenomenon brings us an urgent question: The only research having studied on this question, as far as we know, was R2RIE-CE IROS:Error , which followed VLN-CE ECCV:VLN-CE as the foundation, then artificially injected three types of errors into the instructions, pioneeringly building a benchmark to evaluate a VLN agent's robustness against mistaken instructions. However, we noticed two serious weaknesses: 1) In terms of benchmark, all the 11,764 episodes relied on artificial annotation, which was inefficient and costly to be reproduced on other benchmarks; 2) In terms of method, to detect and localize the instruction errors before starting running, they trained a cross-modal transformer taking camera images across all the time steps as inputs. In fact, however, an agent only access the initial single camera image at that moment. Hence, we suggest a large gap from simulation to reality on R2RIE-CE. To extend the evaluation for agricultural VLN agents and avoid the current weaknesses of R2RIE-CE, we propose the benchmark of Agriculture-to-Agriculture with Mistaken Instruction (A2A-MI), in which we follow A2A as the foundation, then build a semi-automatic data annotation method to insert three classifications of instruction mistake into each original instruction in a more diversified and efficient way. We use A2A-MI to evaluate several state-of-the-art agricultural VLN agents, and observe a sufficient drop on both Success Rate (- 57 ) and Navigation Error (- 9 ), from which we suggest an answer to the question: An agricultural VLN agent tends to assume that the given instruction is correct, so does not have the awareness to doubt it when the scenes it sees do not align with the instruction it receives, unless the instruction mistake is extremely obvious. To build the awareness on instruction mistake for them, we propose the module of Instruction Mistake Awareness and Correction (IMAC), in which we design two core principles to prompt a Vision-Language Model (VLM) analyzing the instruction and the front-facing camera image at the current time step, to judge whether the instruction has mistakes and attempt to correct it when needed. We integrate IMAC into the baseline model, and observe a noteworthy improvement on both Success Rate and Navigation Error, demonstrating the IMAC's effectiveness on strengthening an agent's robustness against instruction mistakes. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose the A2A-MI benchmark, in which every instruction is inserted with mistakes by our proposed semi-automatic data annotator. We test several state-of-the-art agricultural VLN agents on A2A-MI, and observe their poor robustnesses on mistaken instructions. We propose the IMAC module and integrate it into the baseline model, effectively building an awareness of instruction mistakes and an ability to correct them. Related Works A2A The benchmark of Agriculture-to-Agriculture (A2A) arXiv:AgriVLN is specially designed for agricultural robots, consisting of 1,560 episodes across 6 types of scene: farm, greenhouse, forest, mountain, garden and village, in which all the instructions belong to the step-by-step format and the action space belongs to the continuous environment. AgriVLN The agent of Vision-and-Language Navigation for Agricultural Robots (AgriVLN) arXiv:AgriVLN utilizes the Subtask List mechanism to decompose an instruction into a list of structured subtasks, enabling the VLM-based decision-maker only have to focus on a small part but not the whole instruction at any time step, thereby leading to a better navigation performance. Benchmark Task Definition sec:task_definition The task of Agricultural Vision-and-Language Navigation arXiv:AgriVLN is defined as follows: In each episode, the model is given an instruction in natural language, denoted as , where is the number of words. At each time step , the model is given the front-facing RGB image . The purpose is understanding both and , to select the best low-level action from action space , , , , thereby leading the robot navigate from the starting point to the destination. Instruction Mistake Insertion Policy sec:policy We follow all the instructions and images of the A2A arXiv:AgriVLN dataset, then remain all the images unchanged and only implement revisions on the instructions. We categorize human's common speaking mistakes into three classifications: descriptive adjective, concrete noun, and behavioral verb, basically satisfying all the common scenarios in agricultural VLN. To insert a classification of instruction mistake in an episode, we deliberately use a mistaken contiguous span to replace the original one with the same length. An ideal revised instruction should contain both the core semantic and the misleading mistake, i.e., a human can be aware of the exist of the mistake, and can still successfully finish the navigation. Here we share an example to better explain what an instruction mistake classification refers to and how to insert it. Descriptive Adjective refers to an adjective span to describe an object, such as color or shape. A reasonable option is: white green . Concrete Noun refers to a concrete but not abstract object span, such as a plant or an animal. A reasonable option is: signboard billboard . Behavioral Verb refers to a specific low-level action span, such as going forward or turning left. A reasonable option is: go revolve . Semi-Automatic Data Annotation sec:data_annotation To achieve the above instruction mistake insertion policy in a more diversified and efficient way, we present a semi-automatic data annotator, which runs in a two-stage paradigm for each episode. In the first stage, we utilize a Large Language Model (LLM) denoted as to analyze an instruction , to automatically generate a total of three revision candidates for each instruction mistake classification, defined as: where is the prompt template for , which is available in the codes in Appendix. , and are the instruction mistake classifications of adjective, none and verb, respectively. consists of three parts, defined as: where is a contiguous span of length in , and is its revised counterpart with the same length. is the revised instruction. In the second stage, for each instruction mistake classification, we arrange a human specialist denoted as to inspect all the three candidates, to manually select the most appropriate one, defined as: where denotes the candidate selected by the human specialist. Finally, we package all the three selected candidates together with the corresponding image sequence to form an A2A-MI episode. Benchmark Assessment benchmark_assessment We summarize A2A-MI and several mainstream VLN benchmarks in Table tab:benchmark_summary . On the aspects of scene and camera, A2A-MI completely follow the A2A benchmark. On the aspect of instruction, each episode is respectively inserted with three types of instruction mistake, therefore, the final scale of A2A-MI is tripled to 4,680 instructions (only for evaluation) with an average length of 46 words. We further summarize the distribution of mistaken words, as illustrated in Figure fig:distribution . Whether on the adjective, none or verb portion, the new inserted mistaken words are diversified and practical, fully aligning with agricultural workers' potential speaking mistakes in the reality. Hence, we suggest that A2A-MI is a high-quality and large-scale benchmark to effectively evaluate whether an agricultural VLN agent can be aware of instruction mistakes. Methodology In this section, we present the method of Agricultural Vision-and-Language Navigation with Instruction Mistake Awareness and Correction (IMAC-AgriVLN). First, we present the module of Instruction Mistake Awareness and Correction (IMAC) in Sec. sec:IMAC . Second, we integrate the IMAC module into the base model to build the IMAC-AgriVLN method in Sec. sec:base_model . AI.tldr: 提出农业VLN中指令错误感知与纠正模块(IMAC)及对应基准A2A-MI，验证了指令错误场景下模型性能显著下降以及IMAC的有效性。
AI.motivation:
1. 现有农业VLN研究均假设指令正确，不符合真实场景中指令可能出错的实际需求。
2. R2RIE-CE基准存在标注效率低且需全局图像输入的仿真-现实差距问题。
AI.method:
1. 核心思路：在导航过程中引入VLM作为实时错误检测器，对当前指令与前方图像进行交叉验证以识别并纠正错误。
2. 提出半自动标注框架构建A2A-MI基准：LLM生成三类错误候选(形容词/名词/动词)，人工筛选后植入原指令，实现高效多样化错误注入。
3. 设计IMAC模块：利用VLM在每一步分析指令与单帧图像，输出错误片段定位、修正结果及决策摘要，构建即时错误意识。
4. 将IMAC集成至基线(AgriVLN)，使导航策略能够接收修正后指令，而非默认指令完全正确。
5. 关键新意：相比R2RIE-CE需预加载多帧图像，IMAC仅依赖当前单帧，更贴合真实机器人部署条件；且错误注入更可控、可扩展。
AI.result: 在A2A-MI基准上评估多个农业VLN智能体，成功率(SR)与导航误差(NE)均显著下降；集成IMAC后性能显著回升，接近无错误指令时的水平。实验涵盖农业六类场景，属于模拟环境评估。
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值：首次在农业VLN中建立指令错误感知闭环，证明VLM实时纠错机制可有效提升鲁棒性。
2. 主要限制：IMAC依赖VLM的跨模态推理能力，其性能受限于VLM自身对农业场景的熟悉度；错误注入类型有限，未覆盖语序/指代等复杂错误。
3. 关键takeaway：当前农业VLN智能体缺乏对指令-观察不一致的内在怀疑机制，引入显式错误感知模块是必要且可行的方向，但需进一步解决农业领域特定语义鸿沟。

title: AFUN: Towards an Affordance Foundation Model for Functionality Understanding
summary: Affordance understanding bridges visual perception and physical action, serving as an explainable interface for robot manipulation in open and unstructured real-world environments. Yet, building an affordance foundation model that not only understands where and how the interaction should happen, but also generalizes across diverse environments, objects, and tasks, remains a long-standing research challenge. Existing methods typically address only part of this challenge, either localizing task-relevant regions without specifying executable motion, or predicting motion but with limited scalability. In this paper, we present ourmodel, a step towards an affordance foundation model for functionality understanding. From a single RGB-D observation and a language task description, ourmodel predicts a task-conditional functional mask (where to interact) and a 3D post-contact motion curve (how to interact). To support open-world generalization, we build a large-scale standardized data pipeline that converts heterogeneous robot, human, simulation, and real-world scan data into a shared affordance schema with language, masks, and object-centric 3D motion labels. We evaluate ourmodel from three aspects: for affordance segmentation, ourmodel outperforms all baselines by a large margin across 8 test sets from 4 benchmarks, improving mean gIoU/cIoU by +23.9/+26.3; for contact-point prediction, it predicts substantially more accurate points, with a 12.7--61.3% hit-rate gain over the best baseline; and for 3D motion, it achieves the best performance on all three test sets. ourmodel can be deployed for real-world robot manipulation without finetuning for robot embodiment or using task-specific heuristics, demonstrating the ability to adapt to open-world affordance tasks. Project page: https://www.zhaoningwang.com/AFUN
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments Implementation Details sec:exp_implementation We use Qwen3-VL-8B~ Qwen3-VL as our VLM backbone, SAM3~ sam3 as the segmentation model, and Sonata~ sonata as the 3D feature encoder; all three pretrained components are frozen throughout training. The motion decoder uses six transformer layers. Along with the MLPs and MetaQuery tokens, our model adds only 32.21M trainable parameters on top of the pretrained models. We use 64 MetaQuery tokens in total, where each semantic and motion branch has 32. We set , , and train the model with a learning rate of . For the point-sampling loss, we sample points per curve. We train on NVIDIA GH200 GPUs for approximately eight days. The three stages mentioned above use batch sizes of 196, 128, and 96, respectively, and run for 10 , 000, 40 , 000, and 20 , 000 steps, respectively. Affordance Evaluation sec:exp_seg To comprehensively demonstrate the affordance understanding capability of , we evaluate it from three perspectives: accuracy of affordance mask segmentation, correctness of the contact point derived from the mask, and quality of 3D motion. Affordance Segmentation Evaluation We first evaluate 's capability to reason about where the affordance lies by measuring segmentation quality. We compare against three baselines: a zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B~ Qwen3-VL object query generation + SAM3~ sam3 mask generation pipeline, AffordanceNet~ ragnet , and Affordance-R1~ affordancer1 . We show qualitative task-conditioned affordance mask segmentation results in Fig.~ fig:quali_seg . consistently predicts the correct affordance region for the diverse task instructions, can precisely segment complex regions (scissors handle with holes), and strictly aligns with the given task (shovel blade--containing, hammer handle--using), demonstrating superior performance in reasoning about the task-specific affordance compared to baselines. Quantitatively, following our baselines~ ragnet,gloverpp,affordancer1 , we evaluate on eight test sets drawn from four affordance benchmarks, and report gIoU and cIoU metrics in Table~ tab:seg_results . Across all test sets, outperforms all the baselines, achieves the best gIoU and cIoU, and improves overall mean gIoU/cIoU by points over the strongest baseline. Notably, even when using the Qwen3-VL-2B variant with fewer parameters, remains superior to the baseline models by a large margin. Contact Point Evaluation Beyond using masks for affordance, prior work also adopts contact points as an affordance representation; we therefore compare with A0~ xu2025a0 , GLOVER++~ gloverpp , VRB~ bahl2023vrb , and measure whether a predicted contact point lies on the ground-truth affordance mask. For , we take the Pole of Inaccessibility~ GarciaCastellanos2007 of the predicted mask as the contact point. We use hit rate , which measures whether the predicted contact point lies on the affordance mask as the evaluation metric. As shown in Table~ tab:point_hitrate , significantly outperforms the best baseline by -- ( on InstructPart and on ReasonAFF). 3D Motion Evaluation sec:exp_motion3d Evaluation Datasets. We evaluate D motion on three test sets with different domain shifts. (I) The test set ( examples) is a cross-source split randomly sampled from the high-quality set we curated. This test set is further verified through a second human quality-control pass, and we exclude these data samples from the training set to prevent data leak. (II) The SceneFun3D~ delitzas2024scenefun3d test set ( examples) comes from the original validation set in SceneFun3D and contains scenes that are not present in the training set. For each task in each scene, we use the first frame in which the target object is visible for evaluation (details of dataset processing in Appendix~ sec:appendix-data-preprocessing ). (III) The RoboMIND2 dataset test set ( examples) is an out-of-domain test set deliberately excluded from training. We keep functionality-related tasks and remove relocation-only instructions such as ``place A to B'' for evaluation, as such waypaths are usually non-deterministic. Evaluation Metrics and Baselines. We evaluate predicted 3D motion curves using Average Displacement Error (ADE), Final Displacement Error (FDE)~ liu2022joint,yuan2024general computed in both absolute scale and relative scale, contact-in-mask hit rate (CIM). We compare with four 3D affordance baselines: A0~ xu2025a0 , VRB~ bahl2023vrb , VidBot~ chen2025vidbot , and General~Flow~ yuan2024general . For each baseline, we follow their official protocol to obtain the 3D motion predictions, and linearly interpolate every prediction and every ground-truth trajectory to a common length of points for evaluation. Note that General~Flow~ yuan2024general requires manually-specified query points for motion prediction, so we ``lend'' the predicted mask from our model for its query sampling. Evaluation Results. We provide quantitative results in Table~ tab:motion_3d and qualitative results in Fig.~ fig:qualitative . achieves the best ADE and FDE in both absolute and relative scale on all three test sets, and significantly outperforms the baselines in CIM. Even when General~Flow is evaluated under a favorable protocol, as it is provided with 's predicted mask and start anchor, still achieves substantially better motion prediction results. This advantage is further shown in Fig.~ fig:qualitative : produces task-aligned masks and motions, whereas the baselines often produce both implausible object localization and task-inconsistent trajectories. Ablations sec:exp_ablations We ablate three different design choices of our model: the LLM backbone, the 3D feature encoder, and the motion curve parameterization. Results are provided in Table~ tab:ablation-llm and Table~ tab:ablation-motion . For different LLM backbones, we train the model using the same recipe as our default model and report the evaluation performance on all the 8 test sets. Our default model with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves the best segmentation performance, outperforming both the smaller model Qwen3-VL-2B and the larger Qwen3.5-9B. We hypothesize: the reason why larger Qwen3.5-9B underperforms is that its general-purpose MoE design might be less suited to dense vision--language prediction. For the 3D feature encoder, we replace Sonata with the DFormerv2~ dformer architecture and train it using the same recipe. We evaluate the performance on the open-domain RoboMIND2 test set. Our default 3D feature encoder outperforms DFormerv2~ dformer , benefiting from stronger 3D geometric cues in point cloud-derived features. For motion curve representation, we compare our curve parameterization with the representation used in OPD~ opd . Our representation achieves better results, as the single parameterization for multiple motion types in OPD can introduce ambiguity. Real-Robot Demonstration sec:exp_realrobot Deploying on real robotic platforms is straightforward and requires no additional task-specific heuristics. Given a calibrated RGB-D input from one camera, predicts a contact mask and post-contact motion trajectory; the mask is back-projected to localize the target object, while AnyGrasp~ fang2023anygrasp estimates feasible grasp poses from the reconstructed scene point cloud. The predicted trajectory, represented as a smooth spline curve, provides a local tangent direction for adapting the gripper orientation, enabling rotational manipulation such as opening a microwave. This orientation-aware execution is difficult to obtain from line-based trajectory predictions in prior approaches~ bahl2023vrb,xu2025a0,yuan2024general . For each task, uses one RGB-D observation as input, while observations from both cameras are fused into the scene point cloud used by AnyGrasp. We report success rates in Tab.~ tab:task_success_rates and qualitative examples in Fig.~ fig:robotic_demo . achieves an average success rate of 90 , demonstrating reliable real-robot deployment for both contact-centric grasping and orientation-aware articulated-object manipulation.

AI.tldr: AFUN 构建了一个统一的 affordance 理解框架，从单眼 RGB-D 输入同时预测功能掩码和 3D 接触后运动轨迹，并在跨域数据上训练出一个可供机器人直接部署的基础模型。
AI.motivation:
1. 现有 affordance 方法通常是局部能力：或只定位区域不给出可执行运动，或只预测运动但缺乏可扩展的跨域泛化能力。
2. 缺乏统一标注框架与大规模跨源数据，导致难以训练能在开放环境泛化的 affordance 模型。
AI.method:
1. 核心思路是将 affordance 理解分解为任务条件的功能掩码预测（where）与物体中心的 3D 接触后运动曲线预测（how），并由统一模型从单帧 RGB-D 与语言指令输出。
2. 关键设计是构建大规模标准化数据管道，将机器人、人类、仿真与扫描数据统一到同一 affordance schema（语言+掩码+物体中心 3D 运动），支持开放世界泛化。
3. 冻结预训练骨干（VLM、SAM、3D 编码器），仅训练轻量解码器与可学习的 MetaQuery tokens，使模型快速适应多任务而保持强表征。
4. 使用 64 个 MetaQuery tokens 并行输出语义掩码与运动曲线，以单参数化同时表达多种交互类型，避免 OPD 式多分支的歧义。
AI.result: 模型在四个基准的八个测试集上评估：affordance 分割显著超越所有基线（平均 gIoU/cIoU 提升超过 23/26 点），接触点命中率提高 12–61%，并在三套独立测试集上于 ADE、FDE 与接触点命中率均取得最优。真实机器人部署中，无需微调或启发式，在四项任务上达到 90% 成功率，同时支持旋转操作。
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值：提供首个从单眼 RGB-D 直接预测 3D 可执行运动曲线的 affordance 模型，在跨域数据上的统一训练使其具备开放世界泛化与零样本机器人部署能力。
2. 隐含限制：3D 运动预测依赖高质量的物体中心轨迹标注，且当前评价仅覆盖部分交互类型；模型能力上限受限于预训练骨干的姿态冻结与 MetaQuery 容量的约束。
3. 关键洞见：统一的多任务管道与冻结骨干+轻量适配器的架构可高效将 VLM 与 3D 编码器迁移至 affordance 任务，但旋转操作等复杂交互仍依赖额外的姿态适配（AnyGrasp）与轨迹方向的局部切向估计。

title: TERRA: Task-Embedded Reasoning and Representation Architecture for Cross-Domain Applications
summary: A single action-conditioned latent predictive architecture can in principle be trained on the structured state of a driving scene, a robot workspace, or a financial order book. The ingredients for doing so within any one domain already exist and are individually validated: masked-latent prediction, action-conditioned latent world models, discrete action tokenization, and joint-embedding prediction on voxelized state. What is not established, and what TERRA addresses, is the transfer question: when does a representation or predictor learned in one structured-state domain carry over to a structurally analogous but otherwise unrelated domain, and by how much. We give this question a formal treatment. We model each domain as a controlled Markov process on a graded latent grid, factor any instantiation into thin domain adapters and a shared domain-invariant core, and identify a cross-domain correspondence with an approximate Markov decision process homomorphism whose quality is measured by a lax bisimulation discrepancy and, for domains lacking a shared coordinate system, by a Gromov-Wasserstein distance between their action-conditioned transition operators. Under a Lipschitz predictor we derive a transfer bound that separates source-model error from structural mismatch, grows geometrically in the prediction horizon, and is certified from below by the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; we then connect latent error to decision regret through the Lipschitz value property of bisimulation metrics. The resulting Structured-State Transfer Hypothesis is stated as a falsifiable claim with a preregistered experimental program, centered on a transfer test from driving scenes to order books, including conditions under which it is refuted. We present no empirical results: this is a research proposal that converts a widely repeated intuition into testable theory.
full_text: Representation Architecture for\\[0.2em] Cross-Domain Applications Shayan Shokri Humanpath Labs Inc. 0.92 Abstract A single action-conditioned latent predictive architecture can in principle be trained on the structured state of a driving scene, a robot workspace, or a financial order book. The ingredients for doing so within any one of these domains already exist and are individually validated: masked-latent prediction [1, 2], action-conditioned latent world models [3, 8, 9], discrete action tokenization [4, 5, 6], and joint-embedding prediction on voxelized state [14, 15, 17]. What is not established, and what TERRA addresses, is the transfer question: when does a representation or predictor learned in one structured-state domain carry over to a structurally analogous but otherwise unrelated domain, and by how much. We give this question a formal treatment. We model each domain as a controlled Markov process on a graded latent grid, factor any instantiation into thin domain adapters and a shared domain-invariant core, and identify a cross-domain correspondence with an approximate Markov decision process homomorphism [21, 23, 24] whose quality is measured by a lax bisimulation discrepancy [24, 27] and, at the level of whole domains lacking a shared coordinate system, by a Gromov-Wasserstein distance between their action-conditioned transition operators [29]. Under a Lipschitz predictor we derive a predictive transfer bound that separates source-model error from structural mismatch, grows geometrically in the prediction horizon, and is certified from below by the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; we then connect latent error to decision regret through the Lipschitz value property of bisimulation metrics [21, 22, 25]. The resulting Structured-State Transfer Hypothesis is stated as a falsifiable claim with a preregistered experimental program, centered on a transfer test from driving scenes to order books, including the conditions under which the claim is refuted. We present no empirical results: this is a research proposal whose contribution is to convert a widely repeated intuition into testable theory. ] Introduction The claim that a predictive model of structured state in one domain captures something reusable about decision-making in another is repeated frequently and tested almost never. Action-conditioned latent predictors now work within individual domains. V-JEPA 2-AC [3] plans on a physical robot from rollouts in representation space; joint-embedding prediction yields strong features on point clouds [14] and on LiDAR occupancy grids [17]. Each of these is a within-domain result. The promise that the same architecture, or even the same learned representation, carries from a physical scene to a nonphysical structured system such as a market microstructure or a power grid is asserted widely, yet it is supported by neither a theory of when it should hold nor an experiment establishing whether it does. TERRA takes the position that this transfer question is the open problem worth solving, and that it is answerable with existing mathematical tools rather than left as an intuition. Our contributions are the following. [leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] A formal model of a structured-state decision domain as a controlled Markov process on a graded latent grid (Section 3), and a factorization of any instantiation into domain adapters and a shared domain-invariant core (Section 4). A theory of cross-domain correspondence (Section 5) that identifies the correspondence between two domains with an approximate Markov decision process homomorphism, measures its quality by a lax bisimulation discrepancy and a Gromov-Wasserstein distance between transition operators, and derives a predictive transfer bound separating source-model error from structural mismatch. A reduction from latent prediction error to decision regret using the Lipschitz value property of bisimulation metrics, so that the bound speaks to control quality and not only to representation fidelity. The Structured-State Transfer Hypothesis, stated as a falsifiable empirical claim, and a preregistered experimental program with explicit refutation conditions (Section 8). We use the architecture of an existing structured-state predictor, retained under the TERRA name, as a concrete substrate that realizes the interface (Section 6). The substrate is a recombination of validated components and is presented as engineering. The theory of transfer built on top of it is the contribution. Related Work and Positioning We position TERRA against two bodies of work: the predictive-learning lineage it uses as a substrate, and the abstraction-theory lineage on which the transfer analysis rests. Predictive-learning substrate. I-JEPA [1] and V-JEPA [2] established masked prediction in representation space following the program of LeCun [11]. V-JEPA 2-AC [3] adds action conditioning and plans on a real robot. DINO-WM [9], PLDM [10], Dreamer [8], and the original world model of Ha and Schmidhuber [7] form the action-conditioned world-modeling line; RT-2 [4], OpenVLA [5], and [6] supply discrete action tokenization; BYOL [12] and masked autoencoding [13] supply the anti-collapse and masking machinery; Point-JEPA [14], 3D-JEPA [15], GeoMAE [16], and the LiDAR occupancy world model [17] bring all of this to voxelized state, the substrate domain TERRA itself uses. None of these components is claimed as novel here. Abstraction theory. Markov decision process homomorphisms [23] and bisimulation metrics [21, 22] formalize when two states, or two processes, are behaviorally equivalent, and they come with value-preservation guarantees. The lax bisimulation metric [24] extends this to abstract over actions and is exactly the relation realized by a homomorphism. DeepMDP [25] and deep bisimulation for control [26] learn latent spaces in which embedding distance upper-bounds bisimulation distance. Continuous homomorphisms with policy-gradient guarantees [27] and a generalized bisimulation metric between pairs of distinct processes [28] extend the theory to the cross-process setting that transfer requires. We use these tools, together with the Gromov-Wasserstein distance between metric-measure spaces [29], to make the cross-domain correspondence quantitative. What remains open. None of the predictive-learning work tests transfer across the boundary from physical to nonphysical domains, and none of the abstraction-theory work has been instantiated for high-dimensional action-conditioned latent predictors over structured grids. TERRA joins the two. Structured-State Decision Domains [Structured-state domain] A structured-state decision domain is a tuple where the state space is a Polish space admitting a graded grid representation ; the action space admits a discrete tokenization over a finite vocabulary ; is a transition kernel; and is a bounded task signal. A driving scene is a voxel grid over physical space; an order book is a grid over price, time, and side; a risk portfolio is a grid over assets and factors. We call admissible when all four elements are present and is learnable from logged trajectories. Admissibility is a property of the domain and not of any model. The Domain-Invariant Interface The interface is what makes transfer measurable rather than rhetorical. We factor any instantiation into two parts. The domain adapters, which are small and domain-specific, comprise an encoder front-end mapping the grid into a canonical latent space , together with the tokenizer . The shared core, which is large and domain-invariant, comprises a context-encoder trunk , an exponential-moving-average target encoder , and an action-conditioned latent predictor that operates only on canonical latents and action tokens. Because the core is identical across domains by construction, any transfer that is observed when the core trained on one domain is reused on another is attributable to shared structure rather than to architecture reuse. This is the property the theory below exploits. Cross-Domain Transfer We work throughout in the canonical latent space of each domain. AI.tldr: terrar 提出将跨领域结构化状态建模形式化为近似马尔可夫决策过程同态与松弛双模拟问题，并给出了可证伪假设与预注册实验方案。
AI.motivation:
1. 现有的动作条件 latent 预测架构仅验证单域内可行性，缺乏跨领域迁移的理论框架与实验证据
2. 从物理场景向金融订单簿等非物理结构化系统的表示迁移仍停留在直觉层面，未建立可检验的因果关系
AI.method:
1. 将每个结构化状态域建模为分级 latent 网格上的受控马尔可夫过程，并分解为薄层域适配器与共享域不变核心
2. 将跨域对应定义为近似 MDP 同态，以松弛双模拟差异度量局部对应质量，以 Gromov-Wasserstein 距离度量全局结构相似性
3. 在 Lipschitz 预测器假设下推导预测误差的可分解转移界，随预测视野几何增长，并由 Gromov-Wasserstein 距离给出下限
4. 通过双模拟度量的 Lipschitz 值性质将 latent 预测误差下界转化为决策遗憾，连接表示质量与控制性能
AI.result: terrar 未提供任何实验结果，仅给出理论框架与预注册的实验方案，核心验证将从驾驶场景向金融订单簿进行迁移测试
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值在于将跨领域结构化状态推理的直觉转化为可证伪的数学理论与可量化迁移性边界
2. 主要限制在于理论依赖 Lipschitz 预测器、域可分解性以及 canonical latent 归一化等强假设，实际系统可能不满足
3. 关键 takeaway 是迁移性的理论上限由 Gromov-Wasserstein 距离决定，且几何增长误差界意味着核心的动态稳定性直接影响可迁移视野

title: Goal2Pixel: Grounding Goals to Pixels for Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a common foundation for vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE). Yet most VLM-based methods cast navigation as low-level action prediction, an interface that is ambiguous, tied to short-horizon motion primitives, and inefficient due to repeated VLM querying. We propose Goal2Pixel, a pure pixel-based paradigm that reformulates VLN-CE as navigable pixel grounding. Rather than predicting actions, Goal2Pixel uses the image plane as a unified spatial interface between VLM reasoning and robot motion: the model predicts a visible navigable pixel to the agent, which is back-projected into a 3D waypoint for forward navigation. For non-forward actions, we append auxiliary directive regions to the image plane, where the left/right/bottom regions are interpreted as turning left, turning right, and stopping, respectively. To enable long-horizon navigation, we propose a visibility-aware keyframe memory for compact and informative history representation. To adapt pretrained VLMs to navigable pixel grounding, we introduce semantic embeddings and coordinate-aware auxiliary losses. Goal2Pixel achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance while requiring fewer VLM inference calls than prior methods. On R2R-CE Val-Unseen it achieves 54.1% SR and 52.5% SPL with just 7.75 VLM calls per episode, 6x fewer than the 46.62 required by direct action prediction at 32.9% SR. The same trend holds on RxR-CE.Project Page: https://baobao0926.github.io/Goal2Pixel/.
full_text: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a common foundation for vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE). Yet most VLM-based methods cast navigation as low-level action prediction, an interface that is ambiguous, tied to short-horizon motion primitives, and inefficient due to repeated VLM querying. We propose Goal2Pixel, a pure pixel-based paradigm that reformulates VLN-CE as navigable pixel grounding. Rather than predicting actions, Goal2Pixel uses the image plane as a unified spatial interface between VLM reasoning and robot motion: the model predicts a visible navigable pixel to the agent, which is back-projected into a 3D waypoint for forward navigation. For non-forward actions, we append auxiliary directive regions to the image plane, where the left/right/bottom regions are interpreted as turning left, turning right, and stopping, respectively. To enable long-horizon navigation, we propose a visibility-aware keyframe memory for compact and informative history representation. To adapt pretrained VLMs to navigable pixel grounding, we introduce semantic embeddings and coordinate-aware auxiliary losses. Goal2Pixel achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance while requiring fewer VLM inference calls than prior methods. On R2R-CE Val-Unseen it achieves 54.1 SR and 52.5 SPL with just 7.75 VLM calls per episode, 6× fewer than the 46.62 required by direct action prediction at 32.9 SR. The same trend holds on RxR-CE. Project Page . Introduction Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) r2r-ce, rxr requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and reach a target through fine-grained physical movements. Unlike static vision-language understanding, VLN-CE is a language-conditioned spatial decision-making problem: the agent must ground language in egocentric observations, track its progress, and continuously decide where to move next vln_bert, hamt, fgr2r, know_where . Vision-language models (VLMs) internvl, qwen25vl, vila, llava offer a natural foundation for this problem, and recent VLN-CE methods increasingly build on pretrained VLMs to improve instruction-following and generalization efficientVLN, Janusvln, Uni-navid, correctnav, navid, NaviLLM, nav-r1, vln-r1, Navila, Mapnav, navcot, LH-VLN . Yet the interface between this high-level reasoning and executable motion has barely evolved: most VLM-based methods still query the VLM at every timestep for low-level meta-actions such as turn left/right 15°, move forward 25 cm, or stop. This action-centric interface in VLN-CE has three fundamental limitations. (i) Ambiguous action supervision: many distinct action sequences can reach the same goal, making the oracle trajectory an unnecessarily restrictive training target r2r-ce, krantz2021waypoint, narrowthegap . (ii) Myopic decisions: optimizing for the next short-range movement instead of longer-horizon spatial reasoning krantz2021waypoint . (iii) High inference cost: because each prediction advances the agent only a few centimeters or degrees, the VLM must be invoked dozens of times per episode navid, Janusvln, Streamvln, Uni-navid . Therefore, the bottleneck is not only the capacity of the VLM but the interface through which its reasoning becomes motion. We therefore ask: what should serve as the interface between VLM reasoning and executable motion in VLN-CE? Our answer is the image plane itself, the VLM's native input, where a single pixel can ground a forward navigation pixel in the visual observation and be back-projected into a 3D waypoint for execution. While recent work dualvln has explored the feasibility of pixel-based decisions in VLN-CE, it still relies on a hybrid action-pixel paradigm rather than treating pixel prediction as the unified navigation interface to deal with non-forward decisions. To this end, we propose Goal2Pixel, a pure pixel-based paradigm for VLN-CE that reformulates navigation as navigable pixel grounding: the VLM predicts a navigable goal pixel, which is back-projected to a 3D waypoint via camera geometry and tracked by a lightweight local planner. We define the ground-truth as the farthest visible navigable pixel along the oracle trajectory, removing ambiguous action supervision and encouraging longer-range decisions. For non-forward decisions, we append auxiliary directive regions to the left, right, and bottom sides of the image, where pixels in the left, right, and bottom regions are interpreted as Turn Left, Turn Right, and Stop, respectively. Therefore, all action spaces are unified in the pixel-prediction interface. To support long-horizon navigation, navigators require memory of instruction-relevant landmarks and visited regions, but existing VLM-based navigators feed 8--32 fixed-interval or uniformly sampled frames efficientVLN, dualvln, Janusvln, Uni-navid, correctnav, navid, NaviLLM, omninav, monodream, Navila , most of which carry little new information while increasing additional computation. Therefore, we propose ViKeyMem, a visibility-aware keyframe memory that adds a frame only when the set of visible waypoints changes substantially and overlays the past trajectory on each retained frame, yielding 4--5 keyframes per 100 timesteps while covering every meaningful viewpoint transition. ViKeyMem requires no new training architecture or additional memory model, and can serve as a general history representation module for other navigation systems. To make navigable pixel grounding effective with pretrained VLMs, we introduce two lightweight adaptations. First, since the auxiliary directive regions and trajectory overlays are outside the VLM's pretraining distribution, we attach learnable semantic embeddings on these special tokens to help the model distinguish them from regular RGB tokens. Second, to better align training with the geometry of pixel prediction, add coordinate-aware auxiliary losses, including numeric and angular terms. We evaluate Goal2Pixel on the continuous versions of Room-to-Room (R2R)~ r2r-ce and Room-across-Room (RxR)~ rxr . Compared with prior methods that also do not use external training data, Goal2Pixel achieves competitive state-of-the-art navigation performance. Our ablation studies further show the pure pixel-based paradigm consistently outperforms action-based and hybrid action-pixel-based output designs, while reducing the average number of VLM calls. We further deploy Goal2Pixel onboard a wheeled robot, demonstrating its feasibility for real-world navigation beyond simulation. Contributions. (1) Goal2Pixel, a pure pixel-based interface that reformulates VLM-based VLN-CE from action prediction to image-space goal grounding; (2) ViKeyMem, a compact visibility-aware history representation; (3) Lightweight adaptations, including semantic embeddings and coordinate-aware auxiliary losses; (4) Goal2Pixel achieves 54.1 / 52.5 on R2R-CE and 48.1 / 44.7 on RxR-CE in SR / SPL. Compared with direct action prediction, our pixel-based paradigm improves SR in R2R-CE by 21.2 points and reduces the average number of VLM calls by about 6 . Related Work sec:related_works Vision-and-Language Navigation. Early VLN benchmarks, such as Room-to-Room (R2R)~ r2r-vln , are built on discrete navigation graphs, where the agent moves between predefined viewpoints. Recent benchmarks extend VLN to continuous environments, including R2R-CE~ r2r-ce with fine-grained control and RxR-CE~ rxr with longer and more complex instructions. Existing VLN-CE methods can be broadly grouped into zero-shot approaches, non-VLM learning-based approaches, and recent VLM-based approaches. Zero-shot methods~ boosting-zero-shot, instructnav, AO-Planner, CA-Nav, LaViRA leverage foundation models for reasoning-based navigation, but often suffer from high inference cost and limited alignment with continuous control. Non-VLM learning-based methods~ CMA, EgoMap, Dreamwalker, Navmorph, etpnav, g3d-lf, Cosmo, sim2real, sim2sim train task-specific navigation policies, frequently simplifying continuous navigation through graphs, maps, waypoints, or low-level action prediction. Although effective, these formulations are limited by less generalization ability Navmorph, vint and accumulate errors enp, minderror during long-horizon execution. Output Paradigm. Recent VLM-based navigation methods~ navid, Mapnav, Navila, Janusvln, Streamvln leverage pretrained vision-language backbones for embodied navigation, but most still follow an action-centric paradigm. Several works have explored alternative output interfaces. NavFoM~ navfom predicts relative 3D coordinates for cross-embodiment and cross-task unification, while OmniNav~ omninav predicts continuous-space waypoints for multi-task navigation. The most related work to ours is DualVLN~ dualvln , which also incorporates pixel prediction. However, DualVLN uses pixel grounding within a dual-system framework and still relies on a two-stage decision process: the model first predicts an action-oriented decision such as turning, stopping, or looking down, and pixel prediction process is triggered only when the first-stage decision is looking down. In contrast, Goal2Pixel formulates VLN as a pure pixel prediction problem. By adding auxiliary directive regions to the RGB image, we encode turning and stopping decisions in the same coordinate space as visible forward targets. As a result, the VLM always predicts a single pixel coordinate as the high-level output, without switching between action prediction and waypoint selection. History Representation. Historical observations are important for long-horizon VLN, as they preserve previously seen landmarks and decision points. Existing methods often construct visual history through simple frame selection strategies. Fixed-interval sampling efficientVLN, dualvln, Janusvln, Uni-navid, correctnav, navid, NaviLLM, omninav keeps one frame every timestep, but it can introduce redundant observations in visually similar regions while still providing an incomplete representation of the whole trajectory. Uniform sampling monodream, Navila and multi-frequency sampling nav-r1,vln-r1 improve temporal coverage, yet they may still retain redundant frames in early stages and miss important intermediate observations between two sampled frames in later stages. Beyond simple frame sampling, several methods use more structured or compressed history representations Mapnav, LH-VLN, navcot, navfom, Streamvln . While these designs improve history modeling, they often introduce additional modules or computational overhead. In contrast, ViKeyMem aims to preserve most navigation-relevant context with a small number of selected keyframes without any complex framework and additional computational overhead. Method Vision-Language Navigation Task Definition Vision-and-Language Navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) require an embodied agent to follow a natural language instruction using an egocentric RGB observation history , at a time step . In the standard VLN-CE setting, the agent acts in a low-level action space . After executing an action, the agent receives a new observation, and the process repeats until the agent outputs Stop. An episode succeeds if the agent stops within the instruction-specified target region. AI.tldr: 提出一种将连续环境视觉语言导航（VLN-CE）重定义为可导航像素定位的纯像素接口范式，用图像平面统一VLM推理与机器人控制，替代低层动作预测。
AI.motivation:
1. 现有基于VLM的方法将导航视为低层动作预测，存在动作监督模糊、短视决策、每次仅移动微小步长导致推理成本高的问题。
2. 历史表示冗余且低效，固定间隔采样保留大量信息量少的帧，未针对导航相关性进行压缩。
3. 早期尝试（DualVLN）虽引入像素预测但仍是混合动作-像素流程，无法用单一统一接口处理转向/停止等非前进决策。
AI.method:
1. 核心思路：以图像平面为统一空间接口，VLM直接预测当前视野内一个可见的可导航像素，经相机几何反投影为3D航点执行前进；转向与停止指令映射到图像周边的固定辅助区域，实现所有决策的像素化统一输出。
2. 关键创新：1）像素化目标定义——以沿示教轨迹的最远可见可导航像素为真值，消除动作序列歧义并鼓励长距决策；2）ViKeyMem历史模块——基于可见航点变化选择关键帧并叠加轨迹覆盖，用极少量（~5帧/百步）保留有效上下文；3）轻量适配——为不在VLM预训练分布中的辅助区域与轨迹覆盖添加可学习语义嵌入，并引入坐标感知辅助损失对齐几何预测。
AI.result: 在R2R-CE与RxR-CE连续导航基准上达到与SOTA接近的导航成功率与SPL；关键结论是Pixel范式在显著降低VLM调用次数（约6倍于直接动作预测）的同时保持性能，真实机器人部署验证了方法在仿真外的可行性。
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值：将高层VLM推理与底层控制解耦，以像素作为统一接口解决动作预测三大缺陷，实现高效长视野导航。
2. 深层限制：依赖精准深度以进行像素→3D反投影，对传感器误差敏感；真值构造依赖投影-重投影一致性校验，在遮挡或动态场景中可能失效。
3. 关键takeaway：导航决策的粒度提升（像素级目标）本身可压缩推理步数并改善泛化，而历史压缩的核心在于“视图变化”而非时间采样。

title: ReSkill: Reconciling Skill Creation with Policy Optimization in Agentic RL
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables LLM agents to improve continuously from environment rewards, yet the resulting policies do not systematically accumulate reusable strategies that generalize across tasks. Modular skills can provide such reusable strategies, yet existing skill-augmented RL methods decouple skill creation from policy optimization, risking adopting skills that conflict with the evolving policy. Inspired by Anthropic's Skill Creator, we introduce ReSkill, an RL-in-the-loop skill creation framework that reconciles skill evolution with policy learning. ReSkill exploits the group-wise structure of GRPO to naturally embed three mechanisms with only marginal additional overhead: (1) an assertion-driven skill creator that diagnoses failures from past experience and proposes conditional, trigger-based skill revisions; (2) within-group rollout sampling that enables controlled comparison of skill versions, capturing which version best supports the policy's ongoing learning; and (3) Thompson Sampling with adaptive discounting to balance exploration and exploitation in skill version selection as the policy evolves. Across several domains, ReSkill consistently outperforms existing memory and skill-based RL methods, with the largest gains on unseen tasks. Analysis of the skill lifecycle shows skills being automatically created, tested, refined, and pruned as the policy improves, demonstrating reconciled skill-policy co-evolution.

Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous agents capable of multi-turn interaction with complex environments yao2023react, liu2024agentbench . Agentic reinforcement learning (RL), where agents are trained from verifiable environment rewards, has emerged as a promising paradigm jin2025searchr1, wei2025webagentr1, da2025agentrlvr , yet the resulting policies do not systematically accumulate transferable problem-solving strategies across tasks. Recent work has shown that modular skills, reusable snippets encoding task-specific strategies, can fill this gap wang2023voyager, zheng2025skillweaver, ni2026trace2skill . A pioneering effort is Anthropic's Skill Creator anthropic2025skillcreator , which automates skill creation through an iterative human-in-the-loop testing process (Figure~ fig:intro_comparison (a)). However, the Skill Creator operates on a static policy at inference time and relies on human feedback. A natural question arises: can we build an RL-in-the-loop skill creation process that dynamically creates and evaluates skills alongside an evolving policy? Recent approaches accumulate experiential knowledge during RL training through memory evolution zhang2026memrl , principle distillation wu2025evolver , and skill distillation xia2025skillrl . However, they adopt external knowledge without principled testing, treating skill creation and policy learning as separate processes (Figure~ fig:intro_comparison (b)). Yet this approach risks skill-policy conflict, as externally produced skills may not align with the evolving policy. Ideally, whether a skill benefits learning should be assessed by testing it during policy training itself. In this paper, we propose , a framework that reconciles skill creation with policy learning. ~embeds the Anthropic Skill Creator cycle into the RL training loop and makes use of the group-wise structure of GRPO shao2024deepseekmath : each training step samples a group of rollouts from the same task under the same policy, allowing us to assign competing skill versions within the same group and directly compare their effects. To orchestrate this allocation, Thompson Sampling thompson1933likelihood with adaptive discounting is introduced to balance exploration and exploitation in skill version control as the policy evolves. Each rollout thus serves a triple role: (i)~policy optimization via GRPO gradients, (ii)~failure diagnosis and skill revision through an assertion-driven creator adapted from Anthropic's Skill Creator, and (iii)~bandit evaluation that accepts or rejects skill versions based on how they support the policy's ongoing learning. Our method introduces marginal training overhead and requires no additional rollout budget. We compare ~against existing memory and skill-based agentic RL baselines on embodied reasoning (ALFWorld) and agentic search (seven benchmarks) across multiple model scales, with additional experiments on coding (InterCode-SQL), web shopping (WANDS), and science discovery (ScienceWorld). ~achieves substantially improved performance, with the largest gains on unseen and hard tasks. The skill lifecycle analysis shows skills being automatically created, tested, refined, and pruned as the policy improves. Furthermore, the co-evolved policy can adapt to new domains (ALFWorld to ScienceWorld) at test time through skill creation alone, indicating that reconciled training develops a general capacity to follow and benefit from new skills. Preliminaries We consider an LLM-based agent with policy that interacts with an environment over multiple turns via a tool engine . Given a task and a skill bank that provides strategic guidance with conditional loading, the agent generates a trajectory , where is the agent's action, is the environment observation, and is the subset of skills whose triggers fire. The learning objective maximizes the expected reward : . Group Relative Policy Optimization ( ) shao2024deepseekmath optimizes the policy using group-relative advantages. For each task , samples trajectories from the current policy and optimizes with a static skill bank , where: is the token-level importance sampling ratio, is the group-normalized advantage, is the clip ratio, and controls the KL divergence penalty (details in Appendix~ app:grpo ). All rollouts in a group share the same task and policy , differing only in their stochastic trajectories, providing a natural controlled setting for comparing skill versions ( sec:design ). Reconciling Skill Creation with Policy Learning sec:method Figure~ fig:pipeline illustrates the overall framework. We first describe how within-group skill testing integrates into training, enabling each rollout to simultaneously serve policy optimization, failure diagnosis, and skill evaluation ( sec:design ). We then present the skill creator pipeline that produces candidate skill versions from ongoing training experience ( sec:skill_creator ). Finally, we introduce Thompson Sampling to allocate rollouts between competing skill versions while maintaining training efficiency ( sec:skill_evolution ). The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~ alg:rerl . RL Training with Within-Group Skill Testing sec:design To evaluate whether a skill benefits the evolving policy, we need to observe how the policy behaves under it. However, dedicated testing rollouts are expensive in multi-turn settings, and training under a single fixed skill bank loses adaptivity as skills change. We leverage GRPO's group structure to address both issues: for each rollout in a group, a version assignment is drawn from the Thompson Sampling posterior ( sec:skill_evolution ), and the rollout is generated under the corresponding skill bank . The ~objective extends by replacing the static skill bank with a version-dependent assignment: where is defined in Eq.~( eq:lgrpo ) and the blue terms denote the components introduced by : assigns each rollout to either or via Thompson Sampling, and is the skill bank under the assigned version. Since all rollouts share the same task and policy , the only variable is the skill version, enabling controlled comparison. At the same time, varying skills within the group builds the policy's capacity to reconcile with new skills. This formulation allows each rollout to simultaneously serves three purposes without additional cost: (1)~its reward provides gradients for policy optimization; (2)~its completed trajectories feed an experience reservoir that drives the skill creator ( sec:skill_creator ); and (3)~its outcome under the assigned version updates the Thompson Sampling posteriors for the accept/reject decision ( sec:skill_evolution ). The total rollout count remains identical to standard . RL-in-the-Loop Skill Creation sec:skill_creator The within-group sampling ( sec:design ) presents a cost free skill evaluation mechanism; this section describes the skill creator pipeline that produces candidate skill versions for evaluation. We adapt the diagnosis-proposal-validation loop inspired by Anthropic's Skill Creator anthropic2025skillcreator , replacing human feedback with evolving policy trajectories and verifiable reward signals from the RL training loop. Full details are in Appendix~ app:skill_pipeline and~ app:triggers . The original Skill Creator requires a human practitioner to supply execution examples for diagnosis. We replace this manual step with a continuously refreshed experience reservoir that collects success-failure trajectory pairs from ongoing RL training, each trajectory is annotated with its skill version label and reward . Since evolves alongside the policy, it always reflects the current behavioral landscape and provides the raw material for the diagnosis-proposal loop described below. Each skill is composed of structured content (situational applicability, action guidance, and counterexamples) with an iteratively refined trigger condition parameterized by type. At each step, only skills whose triggers fire are loaded into the context, yielding the active subset of . Each loaded skill includes a when to use field that describes when its guidance should be followed, allowing the policy to decide whether the triggered skill is relevant to the current state. Rather than only diagnosing individual trajectories, we also build a general failure profile across the entire reservoir. A dynamic assertion set of rule-based predicates is applied uniformly to all trajectories, yielding per-assertion pass rates . An LLM-based analyzer receives these pass rates together with a stratified sample of trajectories and produces two outputs: (1)~a prevalence-ranked failure diagnosis that guides skill revision, and (2)~updates to itself to keep the assertion set aligned with the policy's shifting failure landscape. Given the current skill bank, failure diagnosis with representative episodes, and the tracked history of prior proposals with their accept/reject outcomes, a skill creator agent proposes a candidate version : a coherent set of , , and operations. AI.tldr: ReSkill 将技能创建与策略优化统一于 RL 训练循环，通过 GRPO 的组内结构实现无额外成本的闭环技能演化。
AI.motivation:
1. 现有增强技能的方法将技能创建与策略训练解耦，导致产生的技能可能与正在学习的策略发生冲突。
2. Anthropic Skill Creator 在策略固定的推理阶段操作，依赖人工反馈，无法在策略动态变化时评估技能的实际收益。
3. 缺乏在策略训练过程中系统地、可验证地积累和迭代可重用技能的方法。
AI.method:
1. 核心思路：在 GRPO 的每组 rollouts 中嵌入技能版本竞争与评估，使每次 rollout 同时服务策略优化、失败诊断与技能测试。
2. 利用 GRPO 组内结构：同一任务、同策略下为不同 rollout 分配不同技能版本，通过 within-group rollout 实现受控比较，直接测量技能对当前策略学习的影响。
3. Thompson Sampling 联合自适应折扣：对技能版本采用 Bandit 分配并随策略演化对旧观测进行折扣，平衡在技能空间中的探索与利用。
4. 断言驱动技能创建：从训练经验池中自动诊断失败模式，触发基于条件与规则的技能修订（内容、触发条件），并将新版本纳入组内测试流程。
AI.result: 在具身推理（ALFWorld）、搜索代理（多个基准）、代码（InterCode‑SQL）、网上购物（WANDS）与科学发现（ScienceWorld）等任务上，相较于记忆与技能增强基线取得一致提升，尤其在未见任务上增益最大；观察到技能的自动创建、测试、精炼与剪枝生命周期，表明技能与策略协同演化的能力。
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值：首次实现 RL‑in‑the‑loop 的技能创建与策略学习闭环，以极低开销达成技能‑策略共同演化，并提升跨任务泛化。
2. 主要限制：评估依赖 GRPO 的组内结构，该方法对非组策略或高方差环境可能难以稳健推广；经验池的构建与断言集的稳定性对长程训练稳定性存在潜在影响。
3. 关键 takeaway：技能的价值必须在策略持续学习的过程中动态评估，而非在静态策略上离线测试；将 RL 循环作为技能进化的选择压力是实现可积累策略知识的关键。

title: Rank-Aware Quantile Activation for Motion-Robust Crop Segmentation in UAV Imagery
summary: Motion blur from high-speed UAV acquisition de-grades semantic segmentation on rare texture-dependent classes with high agronomic value. Standard CNNs rely on high-frequency magnitude features that blur destroys, causing statistical erasure of minority signals. We propose Dual Quantile Activation (QAct), a rank-aware block replacing magnitude gating with instance-level rank normalization. Evaluated onAgriculture-Vision 2021 across zero-shot and blur-supervised regimes at multiple severities, QAct is the dominant architectural factor: it delivers consistent mIoU gains over ReLU across both regimes and all severities, with strongest gains on rare structural and texture-dependent classes. Some dominant classes (water,planter skip) show mixed per-class performance under distillation. At moderate blur, zero-shot QAct outperforms distillation-trained ReLU; across all severities, Distill-QAct achieves best performance, confirming rank aware activation and blur-domain training are complementary robustness sources.
full_text: Motion blur from high-speed UAV acquisition degrades semantic segmentation on rare texture-dependent classes with high agronomic value. Standard CNNs rely on high-frequency magnitude features that blur destroys, causing statistical erasure of minority signals. We propose Dual Quantile Activation (QAct), a rank-aware block replacing magnitude gating with instance-level rank normalization. Evaluated on Agriculture-Vision 2021 across zero-shot and blur-supervised regimes at multiple severities, QAct is the dominant architectural factor: it delivers consistent mIoU gains over ReLU across both regimes and all severities, with strongest gains on rare structural and texture-dependent classes. Some dominant classes (water, planter skip) show mixed per-class performance under distillation. At moderate blur, zero-shot QAct outperforms distillation-trained ReLU; across all severities, Distill-QAct achieves best performance, confirming rank-aware activation and blur-domain training are complementary robustness sources. Precision Agriculture, Semantic Segmentation, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV), Motion Blur, Quantile Activation, Deep Learning. Introduction caling precision agriculture demands rapid, cost-effective field monitoring. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have emerged as the primary platform for crop scouting, weed mapping, and yield estimation at field scale~ chiu2020agriculture : they offer high temporal revisit rates and sub-meter ground sampling distance that satellites cannot match economically. However, the operational speed required for coverage efficiency introduces a physical constraint that existing segmentation benchmarks have largely ignored: severe 6-DOF motion blur. At realistic scouting speeds, the camera's exposure integral smears fine-grained agronomic anomalies—localized weed clusters, endrow compaction zones, nutrient-deficiency patches—into elongated, low-contrast streaks. These are precisely the texture-dependent, rare classes with the highest agronomic value. Standard Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), trained on pristine satellite orthoimagery, rely on high-frequency magnitude cues that motion blur physically destroys, causing catastrophic segmentation collapse on the classes that matter most. Current state-of-the-art segmentation models (e.g., HRNet~ sun2019deep , DeepLabV3+~ chen2018encoder ) operate on the assumption of availability of high-quality input data. When deployed on blurred UAV imagery, their performance collapses, particularly for small objects or texture-dependent classes. Furthermore, traditional blind deblurring~ kupyn2018deblurgan, kupyn2019deblurganv2, xiang2024deep is computationally prohibitive for real-time onboard inference and often fails due to the spatially varying nature of 6-DOF (Degree of Freedom) camera motion. In this work, we propose a shift from purely magnitude-based feature learning to rank-aware feature learning for robust agricultural segmentation. The core of our approach is the Dual Quantile Activation (QAct) block~ challa2025quantile : a residual activation scheme that replaces magnitude gating with instance-level rank normalization, structurally renormalizing the spatial variance of blurred features so that minority class signals survive the activation layer intact. Crucially, QAct requires no blur exposure during training — the architectural inductive bias alone provides the robustness. Detailed mathematical formulations are provided in Section~ sec:main . To isolate the contribution of QAct from the contribution of blur-domain training data, we compare four variants spanning two orthogonal axes: activation type (ReLU vs.\ QAct) and training regime (zero-shot clean-only vs.\ blur-supervised EMA distillation). Our central empirical finding is that QAct is the dominant factor across both axes: within the zero-shot regime, QAct gains range from +37 to +66 relative mIoU as severity increases; within the distillation regime, QAct provides an additional +8 to +20 relative gain on top of blur supervision. At moderate blur (Severity 2), zero-shot QAct even outperforms distillation-trained ReLU, confirming that the rank-aware inductive bias can substitute for blur-domain training data under operationally realistic conditions. Our specific contributions are: We adapt the Quantile Activation (QAct) layer~ challa2025quantile for dense prediction tasks. By applying per-instance normalization~ ulyanov2016instance prior to rank mapping, we engineer a Residual Quantile Block that preserves the spatial structural hierarchy of agricultural features independently of global batch statistics. We establish that QAct is the dominant architectural factor for blur robustness, providing consistent gains in both zero-shot and distillation-trained settings across all blur severities, with especially large and reliable margins on rare structural and texture-dependent classes. The QAct gain within the zero-shot regime (+37 --+66 relative mIoU) demonstrates that the architectural inductive bias alone is sufficient under moderate blur; the additional QAct gain within distillation (+8 --+20 ) confirms that QAct is complementary to, not redundant with, blur-domain training data. We translate this architectural advance into a deployment-ready capability for UAV-based precision agriculture. Evaluated on the multi-modal Agriculture-Vision 2021 dataset~ chiu2020agriculture under a physically grounded 6-DOF blur simulation calibrated to operational DJI Agras flight envelopes, zero-shot QAct provides robust segmentation without requiring blur-augmented training data — addressing a critical constraint in field-scale agricultural surveys, where paired clean/blurred acquisitions are impractical to collect at scale. The largest gains concentrate on rare structural (endrow) and texture-dependent (weed cluster) classes that drive variable-rate spraying and yield-loss assessment. Evaluation Framework: Drone Physics The Challenge of 6-DOF Motion Blur To rigorously evaluate the robustness of our proposed architecture, we must first model the realistic degradation conditions of UAV acquisition. Unlike linear motion blur, often synthesized in computer vision (e.g., via simple kernel translation), drone imaging involves complex ego-motion. A UAV undergoes translation and rotation (roll, pitch, yaw) simultaneously during the camera's exposure time . Severe motion blur is simulated using a physically-realistic 6-DOF drone dynamics model at Severity 3 (representing realistic operational UAV speeds), introducing spatially variant directional smearing and photometric attenuation across both RGB and NIR channels. Because the depth of the scene varies (even slightly in agriculture) and the camera rotates, the blur kernel is spatially variant. A weed at the edge of the frame suffers different smear trajectories than a crop row in the center. Consequently, no single deconvolution function can recover the sharp image globally. Additionally, each image is typically captured during a different drone flight. Thus, the test-time image distribution is effectively a complex mixture of diverse motion blur distributions, adding another layer of difficulty that breaks standard magnitude-dependent feature extractors. Simulation Setup for Validation We explicitly note that we do not propose this 6-DOF simulation as a novel contribution. Rather, we utilize it as a rigorous, physically grounded testbed to empirically validate our claims regarding rank-aware feature robustness. To generate our evaluation data, we employ a simulation pipeline that maps blur severity levels (1 to 5) to physical flight parameters. For a given severity, we sample random angular velocities and translation vectors consistent with real-world drone dynamics. We generate the blurred image by accumulating sub-frames, warping the sharp ground truth according to the sampled trajectory. Crucially, agricultural sensors capture multi-spectral data. We apply the same temporal integration trajectory to both RGB and Near-Infrared (NIR) channels simultaneously. This preserves the geometric alignment of the blur across spectra, which is a critical requirement for multi-modal fusion networks. The Residual Quantile Block: Superimposing Rank onto Magnitude sec:main We deploy a residual parallel activation scheme within our HRNet backbone, which we term the Dual QAct block: a two-pathway structure combining a standard ReLU pathway (magnitude-preserving) with a pathway (rank-preserving), summed with a learnable scale: where is a learnable scaling parameter initialized to . The target is a standard normal , superimposing a dense, zero-mean rank-signal onto the sparse rectified magnitude signal. For uncorrupted features ( ), the ReLU pathway dominates; when blur attenuates features into the dead-zone ( ), the pathway circumvents statistical erasure by populating it with variance-recovered rank data, ensuring gradients continue to flow for minority class signals. Statistical Erasure vs Distribution Alignment Fig.~ fig:histogram_proof empirically confirms this mechanism: under severe blur, ReLU activations collapse into the dead-zone ( ), erasing the minority class signal entirely, while QAct's per-instance renormalization keeps the degraded distribution aligned with the clean signal boundaries, preserving gradient flow. Comparison: Blur-Supervised Distillation Baselines subsec:distillation To contextualize QAct's zero-shot robustness, we compare against distillation-trained variants that enjoy privileged access to blurred imagery during training. Both distillation baselines employ a mean-teacher framework~ tarvainen2017mean : a teacher network (exponential moving average of the student weights) processes clean images, while the student is simultaneously trained on blur-augmented inputs. The student objective combines a task loss on both clean and blurred inputs with an soft-target alignment loss~ hinton2015distilling between student(blurred) and teacher(clean) probability distributions, encouraging the student to align its blurred-input predictions to clean-input targets. We evaluate a standard ReLU backbone under this regime (Distill-ReLU) and a QAct backbone under the same setup (Distill-QAct). This comparison isolates two orthogonal factors: activation type (ReLU vs.\ QAct) and training regime (zero-shot vs.\ distillation). If blur robustness were purely a data problem, distillation alone should close the gap between ReLU and QAct; if it were purely architectural, QAct should deliver the same relative gain regardless of training regime. Our results show both factors contribute, with QAct as the dominant and more consistent driver across severities and class typologies. Experiments and Results Dataset and Evaluation Protocol subsec:dataset We evaluate on the Agriculture-Vision 2021 dataset~ chiu2020agriculture, chiu2020challenge , using 8 valid semantic classes after discarding the ambiguous storm damage class. The dataset exhibits severe class imbalance representative of real-world agricultural deployment: macro classes (drydown: 12.33 , nutrient deficiency: 7.43 ) dominate the foreground pixel distribution, while rare structural and texture-dependent anomalies are exceedingly scarce (endrow: 0.85 , double plant: 0.79 , planter skip: 0.19 ). These rare classes carry the highest agronomic value and are the most vulnerable to ReLU statistical erasure under blur. We generate blurred evaluation sets at Severity 2, 3, and 4 using our 6-DOF simulation, spanning moderate to severe UAV motion. Severity 3 corresponds to realistic operational drone speeds (e.g., DJI Agras series at 5--10~m/s, 1/500s exposure). AI.tldr: 提出一种基于分位激活（QAct）的残差模块，通过实例级排名归一化替代幅度门控，使CNN在无人机航拍运动模糊条件下仍能保留稀有纹理类别的信号，实现零样本模糊鲁棒性，且与模糊域训练互补。
AI.motivation:
1. 高速无人机成像的6自由度运动模糊会破坏CNN依赖的高频幅度特征，导致稀有但高农学价值的纹理依赖类别信号在统计上被完全擦除。
2. 传统去模糊方法计算负担重且对空间变化运动失效，而现有分割模型假设输入质量高，在模糊图像上性能崩溃。
AI.method:
1. 核心思路：用实例级排名归一化替代基于幅度的激活函数，使特征信号不依赖于全局幅度分布，保留模糊后本可能落入ReLU死区的少数类信号。
2. Dual QAct块：标准ReLU路径（保留幅度）与排名路径（经实例归一化后映射到分位数）并行，可学习系数相加，使干净输入时ReLU主导，模糊时排名路径接替梯度流。
3. 关键改进：在分位激活前加入实例归一化（InstanceNorm），解耦空间结构层次与全局幅度统计，确保农学特征的相对结构关系被保留。
4. 对比设计：正交排列激活类型（ReLU vs QAct）与训练方式（零样本清洁训练 vs 模糊监督EMA蒸馏），分离架构贡献与数据贡献。
AI.result: 在Agriculture-Vision 2021数据集上，基于6自由度模糊模拟（覆盖操作速度的Severity 2-4）评估。QAct在零样本和蒸馏两类训练框架下均稳定超过ReLU，且对稀有结构/纹理类别增益最大；中等模糊下零样本QAct已优于蒸馏训练ReLU；两者结合（Distill-QAct）达到全程最优，证明排名感知与模糊域训练互补。
AI.conclusion:
1. 核心价值：架构层面的排名感知归纳偏置可单独提供显著零样本模糊鲁棒性，无需收集成对模糊数据，适用于难以采集模糊训练样本的田间作业。
2. 关键限制：方法依赖6-DOF模拟与真实无人机运动之间的一致性；排名归一化可能引入噪声或平滑本不该被保护的背景；对极端模糊（Severity 4-5）的维持能力需更多真机验证。
3. 核心发现：QAct是主导因子，其增益在类别层面与农学价值正相关；架构与数据源的两条增强路径正交互补，非简单叠加。

title: Where to Look: Can Foundation Models Reach a Target Viewpoint Through Active Exploration?
summary: Humans can reproduce the viewpoint specified by a target image through active head and body motion, yet spatial intelligence in foundation models has largely been studied as passive understanding of pre-collected observations. We introduce Target Viewpoint Reproduction (TVR) -- an active task where an agent adjusts its viewpoint in a 3D environment until its observation matches a given target image -- and TVRBench, an indoor-simulation benchmark spanning scene scale and target-view visual richness. TVR is far from solved: on the evaluation split, the strongest open-source and closed-source models reach only 7.8% and 12.0% success. Fine-grained analysis identifies two consistent bottlenecks: off-the-shelf models struggle with multi-turn visual history, and performance drops sharply when viewpoint reproduction requires body translation rather than in-place rotation, exposing a gap in mapping spatial discrepancies to embodied movement. To study reducing this gap, we build a unified TVR post-training framework covering expert-trajectory SFT, rationale-supervised CoT-SFT, offline Single-turn GRPO, and on-policy Multi-turn GRPO from live simulator rollouts. Visual-action SFT supplies the main gain, raising a 9B open-source model to 50.8% success; Multi-turn GRPO provides targeted multi-room refinement and reaches 51.4% overall, while CoT supervision and Single-turn GRPO degrade closed-loop performance. These results establish TVRBench as a testbed for measuring and training foundation models that actively perceive and act in 3D environments. Our code, data, and models are available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/TVRBench.
